content.text:
Based on the evidence gathered, I have enough to propose a fix.

**Telemetry summary:** From 18:20–20:00, the compressor ran normally (current ~11–12A, cabin_temp and controller_reading cycling tightly around the 2°C setpoint). At 20:10, compressor_current_a spiked to 24A (~2x normal draw) while still "running", then at 20:20 current dropped to 0A and compressor_state changed to "fault" — and has remained in fault/0A ever since. From that point, cabin_temp_c and controller_reading_c rise together steadily (2.0°C → 3.9°C over 2 hours), with no divergence between the two sensors.

**KB findings:** No entry directly matches an overcurrent-spike-then-trip-to-zero pattern. The closest entry, KB-003, addresses temperature drift due to controller calibration but explicitly states its fix (diagnostic reset) does **not** apply if the controller reading tracks the cabin probe — in that case the refrigeration circuit itself is at fault and needs a technician. Since our telemetry shows controller_reading_c and cabin_temp_c are identical throughout, KB-003's own caveat rules out a calibration/reset fix here and points toward a hardware-level issue. No other KB entries matched this overcurrent-trip signature, so I'm reasoning primarily from telemetry rather than a fully documented KB match.

input.description: Telemetry shows stable compressor operation (~11-12A) until 20:10, when current spiked to 24A (2x normal), then dropped to 0A at 20:20 with compressor_state locking into 'fault' for the remainder of the window while cabin_temp_c and controller_reading_c climb together from 2.0C to 3.9C (unit no longer cooling). Controller and cabin readings track identically throughout, which per KB-003 rules out a sensor-calibration issue (that fix, diagnostic reset, explicitly does not apply when readings track together) and instead points to the refrigeration circuit/compressor hardware itself. No KB entry directly documents this overcurrent-then-zero-current trip pattern, so this is not a fully documented match -- the overcurrent spike followed by a persistent fault lockout is consistent with a mechanical/electrical compressor fault (e.g., locked rotor, contactor or winding failure) that requires physical technician inspection rather than a remote reset or sensor restart. Recommend a service visit; confidence kept moderate given the lack of a directly matching KB entry.
